summary: Documents Apple's DNS Long-Lived Queries (LLQ) protocol, which extends DNS so clients learn about changes without polling. Apple implemented it from 2005 onwards in products including Mac OS X, Bonjour for Windows and AirPort base stations. In 2020 it was superseded by the standards-track RFC 8765.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8764 documents LLQ, the mechanism Apple used from 2005 to let a DNS server tell a client when the answer to a question has changed, instead of the client asking again and again. Apple has since replaced it with the standard DNS Push Notifications, and this RFC records how LLQ worked and what went wrong with it.

questions: how did apple notify clients of dns changes
subtitle: Apple's way of letting a DNS server push changes to a client, now replaced by DNS Push Notifications.

tldr.problem: A client that wants to know when a DNS record changes has to poll, and a polling rate that is high enough to be timely is also heavy on the network and the server.
tldr.mechanism: LLQ adds an EDNS(0) option to ordinary DNS messages. A client registers a long-lived query with a four-way handshake, the server keeps state for it, and later pushes a gratuitous DNS response when the data changes.
tldr.outcome: The protocol ran in Apple products from 2005 to 2020 and was then superseded by the standards-track DNS Push Notifications (RFC 8765). The RFC exists to record the operational experience and to help implementations move across.

facts.label: Refresh point
facts.value: When 80% of the LLQ-LEASE has elapsed

today: RFC 8764 is an Informational document from June 2020 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It documents a protocol that has been superseded: LLQ was replaced by the standards-track RFC 8765, DNS Push Notifications, and the RFC recommends that clients try DNS Push Notifications first and only fall back to LLQ if that fails.

sections.title: What LLQ Does and Why It Existed
sections.content:
LLQ is a mechanism for extending the DNS protocol to support change notification, so that clients learn about changes to DNS data without polling the server. From 2005 onwards it was implemented in Apple products including Mac OS X, Bonjour for Windows and AirPort wireless base stations. In 2020 it was superseded by the IETF Standards Track RFC 8765, DNS Push Notifications, which builds on the experience gained with LLQ.

In dynamic environments, DNS-based Service Discovery benefits significantly from clients being able to learn about changes to DNS information through a mechanism that is both more timely and more efficient than simple polling. Such a mechanism enables live browses that learn when a new instance of a service appears, learn when an existing service instance disappears, and allow clients to monitor status changes to a service instance. Multicast DNS supports this natively, because when a device publishes or deletes Multicast DNS records the changes are multicast to other hosts on the network. Hosts also send occasional queries to the network, in case gratuitous announcements are not received due to packet loss, and to detect records lost because their publishers crashed or became disconnected.

LLQ is the unicast equivalent of that: a client issues a long-lived query and a unicast DNS server notifies the client about changes to DNS data. The RFC calls this a more scalable and practical solution than polling, because a low polling rate could leave the client with stale information, while a high polling rate would have an adverse impact on the network and the server.

Some problems were discovered in the years of use, and they are listed in Appendix A. That operational experience informed the design of the IETF Standards Track successor, DNS Push Notifications. Since no further work is being done on the LLQ protocol, this specification will not be updated to remedy the problems. All existing LLQ implementations are RECOMMENDED to migrate to DNS Push Notifications, and existing LLQ servers are RECOMMENDED to implement it so that clients can begin migrating. Existing clients are RECOMMENDED to query for the _dns-push-tls._tcp.<zone> SRV record first and only fall back to _dns-llq._udp.<zone> if that fails. Clients SHOULD NOT record that a given server only speaks LLQ and default to it afterwards, since server software gets updated. New client and server implementations are RECOMMENDED to support only DNS Push Notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: On a local network, Multicast DNS already tells everyone when a service appears or disappears. LLQ did the same job for a client that talks to one specific DNS server over the Internet. The server kept the client's question open and sent an unsolicited message whenever the answer changed.

sections.title: The LLQ Option and Its Numbers
sections.content:
LLQ uses the standard DNS message format together with an EDNS(0) OPT pseudo-record carrying a new OPTION-CODE and OPTION-DATA format. Encoding the request in an OPT pseudo-record allows LLQ to be implemented with minimal modification to a name server's front end. If a query containing an LLQ option is sent to a server that does not implement LLQ, a server that complies with the EDNS(0) specification will silently ignore the unrecognized option and answer as a normal DNS query, establishing no long-lived state and returning no LLQ option. A server that does not implement EDNS(0) at all may ignore the OPT pseudo-record or return a nonzero RCODE, though the RFC notes this is mostly theoretical, because pointing a zone's _dns-llq._udp.<zone> SRV record at a host that does not implement LLQ is a configuration error.

The protocol is designed for data set sizes of a few dozen resource records at most, and change rates no more than once every 10 seconds on average. Data sets that frequently exceed a single IP packet, or that experience a rapid change rate, may have undesirable performance implications.

The numbers assigned are the EDNS(0) OPTION-CODE LLQ, which is 1; the port LLQ-PORT, which is 5352; three opcodes, LLQ-SETUP 1, LLQ-REFRESH 2 and LLQ-EVENT 3; and seven error codes, NO-ERROR 0, SERV-FULL 1, STATIC 2, FORMAT-ERR 3, NO-SUCH-LLQ 4, BAD-VERS 5 and UNKNOWN-ERR 6.

The OPT pseudo-records follow the EDNS(0) format: the NAME must be 0, the root domain; the TYPE is OPT, 41; the CLASS is 0, which is allowed because clients and servers need not determine their reassembly buffer size or path MTU to support LLQ, and a recipient MUST ignore the class field if it is 0; the TTL is 0; and the RDLEN gives the length of all RDATA. The RDATA consists of zero or more options of the form OPTION-CODE, OPTION-LENGTH, OPTION-DATA packed together.

An LLQ option holds six fields. The OPTION-CODE is LLQ, 1. The OPTION-LENGTH is always 18, because the option data has a fixed size. The LLQ-VERSION is the version of the LLQ protocol implemented. The LLQ-OPCODE identifies the operation. The LLQ-ERROR identifies errors. The LLQ-ID is a 64-bit identifier for one LLQ. The LLQ-LEASE is the requested or granted life of the LLQ, in seconds. All multi-byte numeric quantities are represented in big endian byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: LLQ is carried inside the extra section of an ordinary DNS message, in a fixed-size option with six fields: the version, which operation is being requested, any error, a 64-bit number identifying the query, and the length of time the query should live. A server that has never heard of the option simply ignores it and answers normally, so a client degrades to ordinary DNS behaviour.

sections.title: Finding the Server and the Port
sections.content:
The client needs a mechanism to determine to which server it should send LLQ operations, and to which port. Some firewalls block direct communication with a name server on port 53 to avoid spoofed responses, but this direct communication is necessary for LLQs, so servers MAY listen for LLQs on a different port, typically 5352.

The client finds the responsible server much as it finds the server for a DNS dynamic update. It begins by sending a standard DNS query for the name of the LLQ with type SOA. If such a record exists, the server MUST answer with that SOA record in the Answer section. If no SOA record with the LLQ name exists, the server SHOULD include an SOA record for that name's zone in the Authority section, for example a query for _ftp._tcp.example.com with type SOA might return an SOA record named example.com there. If the named SOA record does not exist and the server does not include the enclosing SOA record, the client strips the leading label from the name and tries again, repeating until an answer is received. This iterative zone apex discovery is described in more detail in the DNS Push Notifications specification.

Having learned the zone apex, the client constructs and sends an SRV query for _dns-llq._udp.<zone>. An authoritative server for a zone implementing LLQ MUST answer with an SRV record for that name, whose RDATA holds a priority, typically 0, a weight, typically 0, a port, typically 53 or 5352, and a target, the name of the server providing LLQs for the requested zone. The server SHOULD include the address records for the target host in the Additional section, and the client SHOULD query explicitly for them if they are missing.

The client MUST send all LLQ requests, refreshes and acknowledgments to the name server specified in the SRV target, at the address in the address record for that target. The SOA and SRV queries themselves MAY be sent to an intermediate recursive resolver; they need not go directly to the name server. If the SRV query returns a negative response indicating that the SRV record does not exist, the client SHOULD conclude that the zone does not support LLQ, SHOULD NOT send an LLQ request for the desired name, and instead SHOULD use the behaviour for LLQ-unaware servers. Servers should send all messages to the source address and port of the LLQ setup message received from the client.
sections.plainLanguage: A client finds the right server the usual DNS way: it asks for the zone's SOA record, then for an SRV record named after the zone that says which host and port handle long-lived queries for it. If that SRV record does not exist, the client concludes the zone has no such support and falls back to ordinary polling.

sections.title: The Four-Way Setup Handshake
sections.content:
An LLQ is initiated by a client and completed through a four-way handshake. The handshake provides resilience to packet loss, demonstrates client reachability, and reduces denial-of-service attack opportunities. The four phases are: a Setup Request from client to server identifying the LLQs requested; a Setup Challenge from server to client providing unique identifiers for the successful requested LLQs and errors for the unsuccessful ones; a Challenge Response from client to server echoing the identifiers, demonstrating the client's reachability and willingness to participate; and an ACK plus Answers from server to client, confirming setup and providing the initial answers.

A Setup Request is formatted like a standard DNS query but with an OPT pseudo-record containing LLQ metadata in its Additional section. It is identified by the LLQ-SETUP opcode and a zero-valued LLQ-ID. The request MAY contain multiple questions, in which case it MUST contain one LLQ option per question, in the same order, and the client SHOULD request the same LLQ-LEASE for each. Requests over UDP MUST NOT contain multiple questions if that would make the message exceed a single IP packet. A client MUST NOT request multiple identical LLQs, that is with the same qname, type and class, from the same source IP address and port, to avoid unnecessary load on servers, although independent implementations on one device using different source ports, and independent clients behind the same NAT gateway, are allowed. The query MUST NOT be for record type ANY (255), class ANY (255) or class NONE (0).

On success the server's Setup Challenge carries an LLQ-ID, a random number generated by the server that is unique on the server for the requested name, type and class and SHOULD be unpredictable; a possible allocation with minimal bookkeeping is to store the time since the Epoch in the high 32 bits and a cryptographically generated 32-bit random integer in the low 32 bits. The challenge also carries the LLQ-LEASE, the actual life of the LLQ in seconds, which may be greater than, less than or equal to the value requested, according to the server administrator's policy. On error the LLQ-ID is set to 0.

The error codes in the challenge say what went wrong. NO-ERROR means the request was successful. FORMAT-ERR means the LLQ was improperly formatted, and the DNS header error code MUST NOT include a format error in that case, since that would create ambiguity between a valid request sent to a server that does not understand LLQ and a malformed request sent to one that does. SERV-FULL means the server cannot grant the request because it is overloaded or the request exceeds its rate limit, and the LLQ-LEASE must then carry the time after which the client may retry. STATIC means the data for that name and type is not expected to change frequently, so the server does not support the query; the client MUST honour the resource record TTLs returned and MUST NOT poll sooner than they indicate, nor retry the setup. BAD-VERS means the server does not support the requested protocol version, and UNKNOWN-ERR covers any other reason.

The client then sends a Challenge Response, a DNS request with the same questions as the Setup Request and Setup Challenge, and one OPT pseudo-record whose LLQ options echo the random LLQ-ID and the granted LLQ-LEASE. If the setup request failed with a STATIC error the client MUST NOT poll the server for that LLQ and SHOULD honour the resource record TTLs. If it failed with SERV-FULL the client MAY retry after the time indicated in the LLQ-LEASE. If it failed with any other error, or the server turns out not to support LLQ, the client MAY poll the server periodically with standard DNS queries and infer Add and Remove Events by comparing the answers, but SHOULD NOT poll more than once every 15 minutes for a given query, and MUST NOT poll at all if it receives a STATIC error code.

On receiving a correct Challenge Response the server MUST return an acknowledgment with all current answers to the questions, along with additional resource records in the Additional section and an LLQ option echoing the granted LLQ-ID and the remaining life. If there is a significant delay, or multiple Challenge Responses were issued because some were lost, the server MAY decrement the LLQ-LEASE by the time elapsed since the challenge was first issued. If the setup completes over UDP and the answers, additional records and the OPT pseudo-record do not fit in a single IP packet, additional records MUST be omitted, and if the answers still do not fit, answers MUST be removed until the message fits. The answers not delivered in that way MUST be delivered without undue delay via Add Events.

Setup requests and responses from the client SHOULD be retransmitted if no acknowledgment is received. The client SHOULD retry up to two more times, for a total of 3 attempts, and MUST wait at least 2 seconds before the first retransmission and 4 seconds between the first and the second. It SHOULD listen for a response for at least 8 seconds after the third attempt before considering the server down, and MAY then periodically retry the setup at a rate of not more than once per hour. Servers MUST NOT retransmit acknowledgments that do not generate responses from the client, so retransmission in setup is client driven and servers keep no timers for incomplete setups. If a server receives duplicate messages, it MUST resend its reply, possibly with a modified LLQ-LEASE. Servers MUST NOT garbage collect LLQs that fail to complete the handshake until the initially granted LLQ-LEASE has elapsed.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a long-lived query takes four messages. The client asks, the server answers with a random identifier and a lease, the client echoes both back to show it is really there, and the server confirms and sends the current answers. The extra round trip is what stops a spoofed packet from setting up a query, and lets the client recover if a message is lost.

sections.title: Event Responses and Lease Expiry
sections.content:
When a change occurs in a name server's zone, the server MUST check whether the new or deleted resource records answer any LLQs, and if so communicate the changes to the requesters in the form of a gratuitous DNS response sent to the client, with the relevant questions in the Question section and the answers in the Answer section. The response also includes an OPT pseudo-record in the Additional section, containing an LLQ option for each LLQ being answered, and each must include the LLQ-ID, which reduces the potential for spoof events being sent to a client.

Gratuitous responses for a single LLQ MAY be batched so that multiple changes are communicated in one message, but responses MUST NOT be batched if that would cause a message that would otherwise fit in a single IP packet to be truncated, and SHOULD NOT be delayed for the sake of batching by more than 30 seconds, since that would cause unacceptable latency for the client. After sending a gratuitous response the server MUST listen for an acknowledgment from the client, and if the client does not respond the server MUST resend the response, twice, for a total of 3 transmissions, after which it MUST consider the client unreachable and delete its LLQ. The server MUST listen for 2 seconds before resending, 4 more seconds before resending again, and wait an additional 8 seconds after the third transmission before terminating the LLQ. The DNS message header of the response SHOULD include an unpredictable random number in the message ID field, which is echoed in the client's acknowledgment.

An Add Event occurs when a new resource record appears, usually as the result of a dynamic update, and answers an LLQ; the record is sent in the Answer section. A Remove Event occurs when a record previously sent to the client becomes invalid, normally as a result of being removed by a dynamic update; the deleted record is sent in the Answer section with its TTL set to -1, indicating removal. On receiving a gratuitous response the client MUST send an acknowledgment back, a DNS response echoing the OPT pseudo-record and the message ID, sent to the source IP address and port from which the event originated.

Resource record TTLs in answers to successful LLQs SHOULD be ignored by the client. The client MAY cache LLQ answers until it receives a gratuitous announcement indicating that the answer has changed, and SHOULD NOT cache answers after the LLQ-LEASE expires without being refreshed. If an LLQ request fails, the client SHOULD NOT cache answers for a period longer than its polling interval. Records intended to be transmitted via LLQs may have unusually short TTLs, because the records may change frequently and the client's cache coherence is maintained through the LLQ and the gratuitous responses; short TTLs prevent stale information sitting in intermediate recursive resolvers that are not LLQ aware. TTLs of records in the Additional section of an LLQ response, which do not directly answer the LLQ, SHOULD be honoured.

To maintain an LLQ beyond the granted lease, the client MUST send a Refresh Request, which is identical to a Challenge Response but with the LLQ-OPCODE set to LLQ-REFRESH, and returns no answers. The client SHOULD refresh an LLQ when 80% of its LLQ-LEASE has elapsed. As a means of reducing network traffic, the client SHOULD include all LLQs established with a given server in a refresh message, even those not yet close to expiry, as long as at least one LLQ has elapsed at least 80% of its original lease, and the message must still fit in a single IP packet. To terminate an LLQ before its scheduled expiration, for instance when a browse operation ends or the client is about to sleep, the client specifies an LLQ-LEASE value of 0. On receiving a Refresh the server MUST send an acknowledgment formatted like the ACK plus Answers message but with no answers, the LLQ-REFRESH opcode, and the NO-SUCH-LLQ error code if the client attempts to refresh an expired or non-existent LLQ.
sections.plainLanguage: When the data changes, the server sends the client an unsolicited DNS message carrying the new records, and the client must acknowledge it. The server retries if no acknowledgement arrives, and gives up and forgets the query after three tries. The client refreshes the query before its lease runs out, and can end it early by asking for a lease of zero.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Known Problems
sections.content:
In datagram-based protocols, servers may be susceptible to denial-of-service attacks and clients may be subjected to packet storms, so mechanisms are needed to limit the potential for these attacks. The RFC's security section contains no new protocol elements; it explains the rationale behind the elements described above.

LLQs require servers to be stateful, maintaining entries for each LLQ over a potentially long period, and if unbounded in quantity those entries may overload the server. By returning SERV-FULL in Setup Challenges the server may limit the maximum number of LLQs it maintains, and may also use it to limit the number of LLQs for a single name and type or by a single client. This throttling may be a hard limit or, preferably, token-bucket rate limiting, and it is intended to prevent denial-of-service attacks, so it is not built into the protocol explicitly but implemented at the discretion of an administrator through the SERV-FULL error and the LLQ-LEASE field.

On the client side, the four-way handshake demonstrates reachability and willingness to participate, and requiring that gratuitous responses be acknowledged limits the ability of a malicious host to make the server flood a client. Rate limiting by client address limits the number of packets delivered to an unsuspecting client further. A large random ID greatly reduces the risk of an off-path attacker sending spoof packets to the client, containing spoof events, or to the server, containing phony requests or refreshes.

Appendix A records the problems found in fifteen years of use. A Setup Challenge message is identical to an ACK plus Answers message when there are no current answers, so with packet loss, retransmission and duplication a late duplicate challenge looks like an ACK with no answers, which causes the client to clear its cache of any records matching the query. The rule that servers must not garbage collect LLQs that fail to complete the four-way handshake until the initially granted lease has elapsed is, the RFC says, probably a mistake, since it exposes LLQ servers to an easy resource-exhaustion denial-of-service attack. Packing multiple questions into a single UDP or IP packet for efficiency is awkward and leads to error-prone programming, because some requests in a packet can succeed while others in the same packet fail, and fully specifying the handling in all possible cases would be a lot of work to document, implement and test. Having two different ways to deliver the initial answers, in the ACK plus Answers message or in a later Add Event, increases the possibility of programming errors.

Finally, because UDP has no standardized way of indicating the start and end of a session, firewalls and NAT gateways tend to be aggressive about recycling UDP mappings they believe to be disused. A high keepalive rate would maintain the mapping but would largely defeat the purpose of LLQ. Existing LLQ clients therefore use the NAT Port Mapping Protocol or the Port Control Protocol to establish longer port mapping lifetimes, which solves the problem but adds complexity and does not work with firewalls and NAT gateways that do not support them. The RFC presents these problems as a cautionary tale about building an application protocol directly on datagrams without the benefit of a mature and thoroughly reviewed intervening transport layer such as TCP or QUIC.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC explains why the protocol looks the way it does: the handshake stops a flood of fake notifications, the server can refuse queries when it is busy, and the random identifier makes spoofed packets hard to guess. It then lists the problems that fifteen years of use exposed, and notes that the replacement protocol avoids them by running over TLS on TCP instead of over UDP.

messages.label: SETUP REQUEST
messages.note: LLQ-SETUP opcode, LLQ-ID of 0, and the desired lease.

messages.label: SETUP CHALLENGE
messages.note: Carries a random LLQ-ID, the granted lease, or an error code.

messages.label: CHALLENGE RESPONSE
messages.note: Echoes the LLQ-ID and the granted lease, showing the client is reachable.

messages.label: ACK + ANSWERS
messages.note: Confirms setup and returns the current answers.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF THE LLQ OPTION

items.title: OPTION-LENGTH
items.text: Always 18, because the option data is a fixed size.

items.title: LLQ-VERSION
items.text: The version of the LLQ protocol implemented.

items.title: LLQ-ERROR
items.text: NO-ERROR 0, or one of six other error codes.

items.title: LLQ-ID
items.text: A 64-bit identifier for one long-lived query.

items.title: LLQ-LEASE
items.text: The requested or granted life of the query, in seconds.

items.label: SERV-FULL
items.desc: The server is overloaded or the request exceeds its rate limit. The lease field says when to retry.

items.label: STATIC
items.desc: The data is not expected to change often, so the server does not support the query.

items.label: FORMAT-ERR
items.desc: The long-lived query was improperly formatted.

items.label: NO-SUCH-LLQ
items.desc: The client tried to refresh a query that does not exist or has expired.

items.label: BAD-VERS
items.desc: The server does not support the protocol version the client asked for.

items.label: UNKNOWN-ERR
items.desc: The query was not granted for some other reason.
